# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-38 (Extended v242)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 10, and 1784-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Charlemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour, Tuileries, Rue Saint-Jacques, Rue de la Jussienne, Rue Coq-Héron, Rue Bussy, Lyons, Grenoble. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba, Point des Catalans, Ile Ratonneau, Rue de la Loge, Catalans, Madrid, Cape Pharo, Cape de Morgiou, Château d'If. **Timeline: 1814-1820 Marseilles; 1 March 1814 Dantès' arrest; spring Year 10 (1833) current time in English subplot; 30 July 1816 Dantès' prison reckoning; summer Year 10 current time in Chapter 38.**

## English Subplot Summary (through Chapter 38, summer Year 10)

**Established solemn promises**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford (winter Year 9). Eldest daughter of Lura Haskick kept promise made to Nerine Prydenridge: chapel roof repair at Kelmere completed by harvest (winter Year 9). Fewyn gave Havus Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Salcombe (winter Year 9). Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family (winter Year 9). Sebin swore to youngest daughter of Havus Stenworth to repair roof of chapel at Wilholt (spring Year 10). **Harine swore to wife of Sebin Brackick to teach children of Kelmere their letters (summer Year 10).**

**Chapter 34-35 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton thereafter. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus. Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. Havie Prydenridge found work in Staveford, moved there; Isric Thornmere followed her within the month. Youngest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth was apprenticed anew and became a herbalist. Youngest son of Nelan Brackick was apprenticed anew and became a weaver.

**Chapter 36-37 winter/spring scenes and rhythms**: Frost silvered hedges; light went early; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; smoke lay flat over fields; wind carried salt and tar smell; road rutted and puddled after thaw. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Children chased hoop down lane; rain threatened since morning but held off; dog barked at nothing then went quiet; baker's boy late, line at oven grew long. Multiple characters hummed childhood tunes while scrubbing steps. Ismira and Movus fell asleep in chairs before fire caught. **RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. RUMOR—In letter Semor Brackick burned after reading, youngest son of Malis Prydenridge revealed old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar.** Movus Brackick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it; counted coins twice, came up penny short. Isric Thornmere won copper chalice from Gadrek Prydenridge at cards fairly. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.** Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. **Ismira Stenson died that summer from festering wound; buried at Kelmere. Bone compass Ismira owned went to Matho Stenson.** **Son born to Luvie Prydenridge and Semor Brackick, named Brevus Brackick; family lived in Ostcombe. Daughter born to Pelde Stenworth and Sebin Brackick, named Elvie Brackick; family lived in Torton. Son born to Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge, named Madan Prydenridge; family lived in Kelmere.** **Febin Prydenridge packed single trunk and moved from Kelmere to Elmhaven.** **Davus was apprenticed anew and became a mason.**

**Chapter 38 summer scene (summer Year 10)**: Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage; wind carried salt and tar smell; carts loaded with turnips creaked past well; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; frost silvered hedges overnight; rain threatened since morning but held off; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; baker's boy was late again, line at oven grew long; crooked sun chalked on forge wall. **Jotho Thornmere counted coins twice and came up penny short. Yera Stenworth read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half saints. Istho Stenworth complained of aching back. Jotho Thornmere complained of aching back. Ilrald read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half saints. Rinelle Corrley complained of aching back. Elvie Brackick walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Sebin Brackick counted coins twice and came up penny short. Dalis left Torton and settled in Yarlby. Elvie Brackick read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half saints. Sebin bought ribbon at stall and regretted it. Rinelle Corrley and Harine Lindmere talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Kadrek Brackick asked: "Will it rain, do you think?" Harine only shrugged. Elvie Brackick complained of aching back. Harine Lindmere mended torn sleeve by window and said little. Pelde and Harine talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Febin fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Movie Prydenridge spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Pelde laughed at story nobody else found funny. Davus watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly. Kadrek fell asleep in chair before fire had caught. Thizek Stenenridge argued with carter over price of sack of oats in Torton. Pelde Stenworth walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Daughter born to Movie Prydenridge and Thizek Stenenridge, named Kamira Stenenridge; family lived in Elmhaven.**

## Marseilles/Pharaon Subplot (1814-1820): Dantès' Imprisonment and Escape

**Edmond Dantès' arrest (1 March 1814)**: Young sailor jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Reported Captain Leclere dead; would become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Wedding feast at La Réserve with Mercédès; betrothal announced. Danglars and Fernand conspired; Danglars wrote denunciation with left hand naming Dantès as Murat's agent. Magistrate arrested Dantès during feast. Villefort interrogated Dantès about commission to deliver letter in Paris. **Villefort destroyed fatal letter—only proof against Dantès.** Mercédès came to Villefort's door inquiring after Dantès; Villefort closed door. **Dantès was doomed.** Villefort reported conspiracy to King Louis XVIII, received Legion of Honor cross. **Noirtier—Villefort's father—disguised himself: cut whiskers, changed cravat, wore dark brown coat, narrow-brimmed hat, walked past sentries with bamboo switch.**

**Dantès' imprisonment and psychological dissolution (1 March 1814–Year 4+)**: Boarded boat to Frioul; saw Point des Catalans where Mercédès dwelt; reached Château d'If. Locked in bare underground chamber. Marked plaster fragment daily with 30 July 1816 reckoning. Expected release in fortnight; waited nearly four years. Governor transferred; Edmond became number 34. At end of second year ceased marking time. Sustained by pride of conscious innocence, then doubted own innocence, then supplicated. Asked for companion; refused. Gloom settled; rage supplanted religious fervor; blasphemies made jailer recoil. Contemplation of abyss offered strange consolation. **Resolved: "I wish to die." Chose starvation; swore oath.** Cast out food twice daily until had not strength to rise. **Heard mysterious scratching—subterranean workman mining way. Raised eyes to heaven, felt gratitude for piece of iron. "If neighbor would not come, he would go to neighbor."** Worked tirelessly; extracted plaster and stone fragments. **Noted prisoner on other side had ceased labor. After two or three hours, iron met smooth surface—a beam blocking hole. Must dig above or under it.**

**Neighbor appears: Abbé Faria revealed (Chapter 38)**: **Dantès made passionate plea: "Oh, I am a Christian," cried he. "I swear to you by him who died for us that naught shall induce me to breathe one syllable to my jailers; but I conjure you do not abandon me... If you are young, I will be your comrade; if you are old, I will be your son... I shall love you as I loved my father."** **Following night Dantès rose, dispersed fragments, pushed bed back, gave himself up to happiness. At slightest noise bounded towards door; if jailer examined opening, he would kill him with water jug.** **Next morning appeared head, then shoulders, then body of man who sprang lightly into his cell. Man was small of stature, hair blanched by suffering and sorrow rather than age. Had deep-set penetrating eye beneath thick gray eyebrow, long black beard reaching to breast. Thin face deeply furrowed by care; bold outline betokened man more accustomed to mental than physical exercise. Numbered sixty or sixty-five years; vigor in movements showed aged more from captivity than time. Received enthusiastic greeting with evident pleasure.** **Stranger: "I am the Abbé Faria, imprisoned here since 1811; previously confined three years in fortress of Fenestrelle. In 1811 transferred to Piedmont. Learned then that Napoleon had son named king of Rome in cradle. Did not expect this colossus would be overthrown. Then who reigns in France—Napoleon II?"** **Faria imprisoned because in 1807 he dreamed plan Napoleon tried to realize in 1811; like Machiavelli, desired to alter political face of Italy, sought one large compact powerful empire instead of petty principalities. Fancied he found his Caesar Borgia in crowned simpleton who feigned to enter his views only to betray him. Plan of Alexander VI and Clement VII will never succeed; Italy fated to misfortune. Acknowledged: "I am the poor mad prisoner of Château d'If, permitted for many years to amuse different visitors with what is said to be my insanity; should be promoted to honor of making sport for children if such innocent beings could be found in abode devoted to suffering and despair."**

**Faria's scholarly achievements**: **Possessed nearly five thousand volumes in library at Rome; after reading, found one hundred fifty well-chosen books possess all that man need really know. Devoted three years to studying these volumes until knew them nearly by heart. Since imprisonment, slight effort of memory enables recalling contents as though pages open before him. Can recite whole of Thucydides, Xenophon, Plutarch, Titus Livius, Tacitus, Strada, Jornandes, Dante, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Spinoza, Machiavelli, Bossuet.** **Made vocabulary of words known; turned, returned, arranged them to express thoughts through their medium. Knows nearly one thousand words, all absolutely necessary, though dictionaries contain nearly one hundred thousand. Not fluent but could explain wants and wishes readily.** **Made excellent pens from cartilages of whiting heads served on maigre days (Wednesday, Friday, Saturday). Historical labors greatest solace; while retracing past, forgets present; traversing path of history ceases remembering he is prisoner. Wrote work called _A Treatise on the Possibility of a General Monarchy in Italy_—entire work, fruits of thoughts and reflections of whole life, meditated in shades of Colosseum at Rome, foot of St. Mark's column at Venice, borders of Arno at Florence. Will make one large quarto volume. Wrote word _finis_ at end of sixty-eighth strip about week ago. Tore up two shirts and handkerchiefs to complete precious pages. Wrote with own blood for very important notes requiring close attention.** **For ink, dissolved soot from former fireplace (closed up long before his occupancy) in portion of wine brought every Sunday. Better ink cannot be desired.** **Used ray of light entering window and lines traced on wall, in accordance with double motion of earth and ellipse it describes round sun, to ascertain precise hour more minutely than watch would allow; sun and earth never vary in appointed paths.** **Made slender stick about six inches long, resembling handle of fine painting-brush, with one of whiting cartilages tied by thread to end, pointed and divided at nib like ordinary pen.**

**Faria's escape plan and preparations**: **Proposed new escape plan: "We must pierce through corridor by forming side opening about middle, as it were top part of cross. This time you will lay plans more accurately; shall get out into gallery; kill sentinel who guards it, make escape. All we require is courage, which you possess, and strength, which I am not deficient in."** **Explained why did not kill sentinel before: "natural repugnance to commission of such a crime prevented you from thinking of it... man loathes idea of blood—it is not alone that laws of social life inspire him with shrinking dread of taking life; his natural construction and physiological formation——"** **On celebrated escapes: "Since my imprisonment, I have thought over all most celebrated cases. Rarely successful. Those crowned with full success long meditated upon and carefully arranged: escape of Duc de Beaufort from Château de Vincennes, Abbé Dubuquoi from Fort l'Evêque, Latude from Bastille. Then those for which chance sometimes affords opportunity, and those are best of all. Let us wait patiently for favorable moment, when it presents itself, profit by it."** **Once thought of removing iron bars from his window and letting himself down, though would have enlarged it preparatory to flight; discovered would merely drop into inner court; renounced project as too full of risk and danger. Carefully preserved rope ladder of cords between twenty-five and thirty feet in length, concealed behind stone fitting closely at head of bed, against one of unforeseen opportunities chance frequently brings about. Ladder firm, solid, compact enough to bear any weight.**

## Marius and Cosette: Courtship to Death Vigil

**Spring Year 6 confessions through barricade**: Marius revealed orphan status, lawyer profession, father colonel-hero. Cosette revealed convent upbringing, dead mother, father M. Fauchelevent. Éponine died leading Marius to barricade. Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed. Shot broke collar bone.

**Medical recovery and wedding (1 February 1833)**: Doctor declared recovery assured. Learned Cosette was not daughter of old man she called father; another Fauchelevent was real father. Dowry: five hundred eighty thousand francs, constituted legacy by dead person desiring to remain unknown. **Wedding at church of Saint-Paul: Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath. Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration.**

**Javert's death and estrangement**: Javert drowned in Seine. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade.**

**Jean Valjean's revelation and withdrawal**: **Proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Marius shocked, concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Address changed to _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean." Cosette became more gay, less tender. Complete extinction ensued. Neatly clad in black, emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year counted for thirty.** Later confined to apartment, then bed. **Revealed black jet from England, white jet from Norway; invented way of substituting slides; six hundred thousand francs made. Also managed very well with glass goods. Adjured Marius: "Have no fear, the six hundred thousand francs really belong to Cosette!"** **[Heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more... What is frightful is to die without seeing her."** **Lies in cemetery of Père-Lachaise, vicinity of common grave, far from elegant quarter, in deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus.**

## Thénardier's Blackmail and Marius's Confrontation

**Thénardier's discovery and exposure**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right there; claimed twenty thousand francs as price. Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. With agility of monkey, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat.**

**Marius's confrontation and evidence**: Revealed Javert's suicide facts announced in _Moniteur_ 15 June 1832: Javert reported to prefect he owed his life to insurgent who fired into air instead of blowing out his brains. **Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof. Condemned Thénardier as "infamous wretch," "liar," "calumniator," "villain." Noted Marius witnessed Thénardier Jondrette in lair on Rue de l'Hôpital; succeeded only in glorifying Jean Valjean.** Offered twenty thousand francs total, ordered Thénardier to America with daughter; wife dead. **Thénardier set up as slave-dealer in America, morally irremediable.**
